title: The Checklist Factory
coreMove: Design the list for the pressure point, cutting everything that does not earn attention in live execution.
sourcePressure: The source turns to Dan Boorman, Boeing manuals, and simulator learning to show the difference between good and bad checklist design, especially brevity, timing, and usefulness.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version says good checklists are thorough. The real chapter says good checklists are selective, timed, and tested against actual use.

sourceAnchors.name: Dan Boorman
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar names Dan Boorman as the Boeing checklist expert who anchors the design-craft chapter.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Dan Boorman's world treats a checklist as cockpit equipment, not as a dumping ground for responsibility.

sourceAnchors.name: Boeing manuals
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar links Boeing manuals to checklist design discipline.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The Boeing manuals matter because every extra line has to justify the attention it steals in a live cockpit.

sourceAnchors.name: simulator learning
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar identifies simulator learning as part of the chapter's evidence for shaping and testing checklists.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The simulator is where the list stops being a document and starts proving whether hands can use it under pressure.

counterintuition: The best list leaves things out
examples: pilot with headset unless tied to source anchor

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.domain: Anna, an aircraft emergency checklist reviewer
exampleSpecs.audience: safety designers deciding what belongs in a live-use aid
exampleSpecs.stakes: pilots in a smoke event cannot use a bloated page while masks are on
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Anna cuts a seven-line explanation into two cockpit actions and moves background detail to the reference manual
exampleSpecs.firstImage: gray training smoke curling around a simulator windshield

exampleSpecs.domain: Daniel, a hospital code-cart restock designer
exampleSpecs.audience: clinical operations teams building checks for rushed restocking
exampleSpecs.stakes: a cart looks complete but lacks the item needed in the next code
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Daniel moves from drawer-by-drawer inventory to a short stop-point check for expired pads, airway kit seal, and first-dose meds
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 11:44 p.m., Daniel opens a code cart drawer full of perfect-looking plastic

exampleSpecs.domain: Sophie, a ski patrol lead building an avalanche response card
exampleSpecs.audience: outdoor rescue teams designing aids for cold, noisy conditions
exampleSpecs.stakes: a long card cannot be used with gloves while beacon search is underway
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Sophie tests the card with gloves on and removes any item that cannot guide the first three minutes of beacon, probe, and radio work
exampleSpecs.firstImage: wind snapping ice crystals against a red patrol jacket

exampleSpecs.domain: Diego, a restaurant closing food-safety list designer
exampleSpecs.audience: restaurant owners fighting false thoroughness at end of shift
exampleSpecs.stakes: a tired closer signs a long sheet while the walk-in temperature alarm is ignored
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Diego cuts the closing sheet to the four items that can spoil food overnight and moves cleaning reminders to training
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Diego one tray of spoiled fish to stop confusing length with safety

exampleSpecs.domain: Anke, a data center incident checklist owner
exampleSpecs.audience: technical incident teams whose aids get too verbose
exampleSpecs.stakes: engineers scroll past the one customer-impact step while reading incident background
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Anke separates the live incident card from the reference runbook and keeps only isolate, notify, and preserve logs on the card
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Nobody reads this while the alarms are red," Anke says beside the status wall

exampleSpecs.domain: Hiroshi, a ferry bridge officer designing pre-departure checks
exampleSpecs.audience: transport operators balancing routine and live constraints
exampleSpecs.stakes: a long pre-departure form hides the two checks that prevent leaving with a loose vehicle deck
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Hiroshi tests the list during actual boarding noise and moves vehicle latch and passenger count to the last moment before lines are cast
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You feel the deck vibrate as truck tires thump over the ramp plate

skillTargets: place checks at usable pause points

tryThisNowSpec: Take one existing checklist and label each item live check, training material, reference detail, or delete.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
